A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same asynchronous SNN simulation and unlayered-backpropagation study. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison despite the changed title and extensive revision.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on N-MNIST, SHD, and DVS gesture, including accuracy, spike density, latency, hyperparameter sensitivity, and training resource use.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds CIFAR-10 results, convergence analyses, and synaptic-operation and projected-energy results.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1, unlayered backpropagation, and the RS/MS scheduling policies remain. The CIFAR-10 extension adapts the model to a convolutional VGG-style architecture with non-leaking IF neurons, continuous-valued inputs, and terminal membrane-potential classification instead of spike-count classification (Sections 3.2, A.4, A.10). These are limited procedural adaptations.

E1.justification: v2 adds CIFAR-10 natural-color object classification to the retained neuromorphic digit, speech, and gesture tasks. This extends evaluation beyond event-stream datasets to static images supplied as continuous-valued currents in one timestep, materially broadening the represented data and input conditions.

E2.justification: Corresponding experiments retain the layered-training baseline and unlayered RS/MS approaches. The new CIFAR-10 comparisons reuse these approaches. Newly discussed methods such as the Yao et al. approaches are not evaluated as additional baselines.

E3.justification: v2 introduces a distinct CIFAR-10 protocol with a VGG-style model, single-timestep inputs, 150 epochs, batch size 64, and forward-group sizes 512 during training and 64 during testing (Table 6; Appendix A.10). It also adds synaptic-operation counts and energy projections using 26 pJ per operation, excluding static power. Settings for the original three datasets remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The original hyperparameter and resource analyses are retained. v2 adds training-loss convergence comparisons for the three original datasets (Figure 10), plus CIFAR-10 inference-group-size sensitivity and momentum-noise stability analyses (Figures 7 and 12). These extend the existing analyses and identify unstable training at smaller momentum-noise values.

E5.justification: Both versions use the same 25th/75th-percentile bars for spike distributions in v1 Figure 2/v2 Figure 4. Neither reports repeated-training run counts or seeds, and v2 introduces no new confidence intervals, significance tests, or run-level uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: The original Table 2 scores and resource-use results are retained. New CIFAR-10 results report accuracies of 0.805 for layered execution, 0.183 for asynchronous execution of the layered-trained model, and 0.712 after asynchronous training (Figure 7). v2 also adds convergence findings and projected-energy entries, such as N-MNIST energy of 0.9155 versus 0.3454 microjoules for layered versus unlayered-RS models (Table 3).

T1.justification: Appendix A.4 extends the mathematical definition of the class logit c_i: for CIFAR-10 it is the terminal output-neuron membrane potential rather than the spike count. The existing backpropagation derivation, neuron equations, surrogate, loss expression, and linear complexity argument remain; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: v2 narrows the abstract's accuracy claim from consistently superior performance to competitive or better performance, and presents the remedy as a potential solution direction. The central synchronization-mismatch claim and headline bounds of approximately 50% fewer spikes, twice-faster inference, and 10% higher accuracy remain.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands explanations of scheduling, relative event order, and hardware dynamics (Section 5; Appendix A.5.1). It develops the training-cost versus asynchronous-robustness tradeoff using the constrained CIFAR-10 experiment and distinguishes projected dynamic energy from static-power effects (Section 4.6; Appendix A.11). These add substantive mechanisms and applicability limits beyond v1's brief discussion.

D1.justification: v2 supplies source-code access information absent from v1 and documents the CIFAR-10 architecture, hyperparameters, memory-driven adaptations, and momentum-noise settings (Table 6; Appendix A.10; Figure 11). It also expands input-encoding documentation. The repository's actual accessibility is not established by the PDFs.

R1.justification: v2 adds a substantive comparison with Yao et al. (2024, 2025), contrasting burst-based approaches with removing synchronization barriers. It adds positioning around newer training methods, neuron models, and hardware, while removing several earlier asynchronous-simulation and synchronization references. This goes beyond the change from numbered to author-year citations.

P1.justification: The introduction and methodological explanations are extensively rewritten, accelerator background moves into Related work, and timing and scheduling terminology receive expanded explanations. The short discussion becomes a substantially reorganized Discussion & Future outlook. These changes extend well beyond inserting new experimental content.

P2.justification: v2 adds synchronization and backpropagation diagrams, an input-encoding illustration, CIFAR-10 and convergence displays, an architecture diagram, and an energy table. It redraws v1's threshold illustration, rearranges retained plots and tables, moves the latency legend outside the panels, and adopts a different journal layout.

improvement.justification: The CIFAR-10/VGG experiment addresses v1's lack of validation beyond small fully connected models and exposes incomplete accuracy recovery and training instability. Clearer diagrams, implementation documentation, and code-access information substantially improve assessability. The energy projections explicitly state their assumptions. CIFAR-10 still falls below layered accuracy, and hardware-energy measurements and run-level uncertainty remain absent, but the broader evidence and clearer limits substantially strengthen the paper.
